Hi @ks00x,

We took a bit of time to think about this, and in version 0.89.0 (due to be released soon, most likely tomorrow), the semantics of keyed widgets will change so that session state keys corresponding to widgets will only be present in the `st.session_state` dictionary if the widget exists as well. Because of this, you'll need to explicitly set `st.session_state` keys to have the values persist to achieve the behavior you're looking for.

This is a bit of a change from the current behavior (which didn't quite work as expected due to the bug described in this issue), but we decided to have things behave this way so that the semantics between keyed and unkeyed widgets are identical (that is, widget values are not persisted in either case if the widget is not present in the app).

Hi @shashankdeshpande,

The behavior you want can be achieved by storing the saved values in a session_state key and setting the value of the `st.multiselect` widget via session_state as well (using a different key name).

```python
import streamlit as st

if "saved_items" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["saved_items"] = []

if "selected_items" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["selected_items"] = st.session_state["saved_items"]

page = st.sidebar.radio(
    label="Navigate",
    options=["page 1", "page 2"],
)

if page == "page 1":
    st.write("this is page 1")
    selected_items = st.multiselect(
        label="Select items",
        options=["item 1", "item 2", "item 3"],
        key="selected_items",
    )
    st.session_state["saved_items"] = selected_items
else:
    st.write("this is page 2")
```

This code works because it's possible to set values of a widget via `st.session_state` using matching keys, and the `session_state` key corresponding to a widget lives only while the widget exists on the page.

I feel like this solution is a bit unsatisfactory, though, given how verbose it is, so I'll think about this a bit more to see if I can come up with a less boilerplate-y way of writing this.

Hey @Bomme, the reason for this is because Streamlit Apps are currently loaded as iframes in Streamlit Cloud and query parameters are not directly added to the iframe's URL, but passed as a message to the iframe. Now, when the app is loaded and the iframe is reachable, the app is executed for the first time. When the query parameters are passed from Cloud to the App, a re-run is triggered. This explains why an app is executed twice.
I agree that the fact that an app behaves differently when deployed to Cloud can be confusing; though, right now, I cannot say whether and when this behavior will change, but I hope this anyways sheds some light on it 🙂

The reason for this behaviour is that the unique widget key is based on the value parameter. Since both options arrays are the same in the second snippet, Streamlit is unable to detect that there is a new widget. The best way to fix this is to set your own widget key that incorporates information from the selectbox, for example:

```python
options = {"a": ["1", "2", "3"], "b": ["1", "2", "3"]}
main_option = st.sidebar.selectbox("A or B", sorted(options))
other_options = st.sidebar.multiselect(
    "numbers",
    ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"],
    default=sorted(
        options[main_option],
    ),
    key="numbers " + main_option,
)
```

Hi @sg-s,

I think isn't quite an issue with either `streamlit` or `streamlit_javascript`. What's probably happening here is that, without the sleep, the two `st_javascript` commands run so quickly that the second call to `st_javascript` is the one that actually gets passed to the component as a prop. In this case, that's the `st_javascript("localStorage.current_streak;")` line (since callbacks are run before the main script run). We can't do too much to prevent this given that `st_javascript` is implemented as a custom component, so it's technically a react component (even though there's nothing visually displayed), which means that react may decide to only "render" the component once with its most recent props. 

This could probably be fixed on the `st_javascript` side by teaching the component to save each prop passed to it in some form of state to ensure that no commands ever get dropped, but doing so would be up to the component author.

Alternatively, changing your code to initialize `st.session_state.current_streak` by doing something like
```python
if 'current_streak' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.current_streak = int(st_javascript("localStorage.current_streak;"))
```
would prevent the calls to `st_javascript` used to initialize `st.session_state.current_streak` in the main script from overwriting the the calls to update the value in localStorage.

Hi @plynch-chwy,

The root cause of this is that widgets don't handle arguments with non-primitive values very well, and what's tripping streamlit up is the lambda function since it gets redefined every script run, which confuses some equality checks. Two workarounds for this exist

* Make the `pages` list a dict, and only pass selectbox the page titles. Then, use the returned page title to index into the pages dict to grab the correct page function.
* Define the `format_func` passed to the selectbox in a separate module so that it doesn't get redefined with each script run.

As a side note, we released [native multi-page app support](https://blog.streamlit.io/introducing-multipage-apps/) for streamlit in June, so it may be possible to rework this custom implementation to use the new functionality.

Going to close this as a duplicate as the root-cause is identical to that of #3703.

This doesn't seem like a Streamlit bug to me. The cause of your issue is that Python imports only ever interpret a file a single time, and subsequent times a module is imported pull the module's exported symbols out what's essentially a global dict rather than interpreting the file again. I'm guessing if you added other fields to session state, you'll find that they should vary independently per-session.

Hi @aarchiba,

This is expected behavior -- the way that widget identity works is that a widget's ID is generated using the arguments passed to the widget, so what's happening in this case is that the streamlit web client sees the slider with the random initial value as a "new" slider. See point four in the [advanced widget semantics documentation](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/widget-semantics).

The standard way of doing something like this would be to use `st.session_state` to set the initial value of the widget via a key:

```python
import numpy as np
import streamlit as st

if "random" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.random = np.random.uniform(0, 100)


r1 = st.slider("Fixed initial value", min_value=0.0, max_value=100.0, value=50.0)
print(f"{r1=}")
r2 = st.slider(
    "Random initial value",
    min_value=0.0,
    max_value=100.0,
    key="random",
)
print(f"{r2=}")
```

Hey @JovanVeljanoski ! Thank you for submitting the bug. The problem here is an unfortunate complexity of session state, but essentially:

To explain the issue:

- The select box's `index` value is always changing. This confuses Streamlit into thinking there's a _new_ selectbox rather than the same one.
- The solution is to remove the `index` parameter and add a `key` equal to `"freq"`, `"color"` and `"lw"` respectively.

Multipage apps makes it complex because once the widget goes away, the value from session state eventually has to.

The more complex solution is, do the above, but:
- Make the key something consistent, `freq_w`, `color_w`, `lw_w`
- Any set to session state on the page should also set the widget itself. So

```python
# in app with respective widgets:

# The widget hasn't been initialized yet, so initialize it with the value from session state.
if key in st.session_state and f"{key}_w" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state[f"{key}_w"] = value
```

There might be some nuances that make your app different. Multipage apps have made session state more complicated and we are discussing solutions here.

Going to close because the current behavior is intended, but feel free to comment if you see any other issues! :-)

@kwkan-dare Thanks for reporting this! This is an expected behavior in the current version. Depending on the use case, sometimes it's more useful to have the fully edited data structure and sometimes it's better to only access the actual edits. Therefore, we decided to return the edited datastructure and only keep the edits in the sessions state (see the advanced docs [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/library/advanced-features/dataframes#access-edited-data)). Another reason why we decided to do this is that it is a lot more memory efficient. If we would add the fully edited datastrucutre to the session state as well, we would need to duplicate the dataframe. But we might change this in the future if we have more users reporting this as an issue. 

Btw. the data in the session state is a TypedDict, which is basically just a dict with better typing hints.

We encountered the same issue in a multi-page application with streamlit 1.26.0 , python 3.10.13 (the python:3.10-slim docker image in a Kubernetes cluster).

The scenario is:
1. A user loads the main page of the application, streamlit opens a new Thread and runs main.py
2. That main page needs to know the window height. We use a react component for that which runs in the background (a separate iframe I guess). That component will trigger a page rerun when the state.window_height differs from the actually detected window height. (this only happens one time, as the state will get updated with the detected window height)
3. Apparently, that rerun will open a separate streamlit Thread also running main.py so there are now two Threads running main.py for the same user/session.
4. We found that:
    - Python switches from the first Thread to the second Thread when the first one is executing a list comprehension (in our case fetching info from an s3 bucket object, but that's probably not related as other s3 actions don't have the same effect)
    - Later Python will switch back to the first Thread and continues the list comprehension. 
    - At that point in the first Thread, the state object will be an empty dictionary.

We can simulate this consistently.

So:
- this happens with one page only, our app has more pages but these aren't rendered at all in this scenario
- the user has only one tab open, but as I said the react component triggers a second Thread (// ScriptRunner)

Hey @jkneer, thank you for opening this issue!

you are correct, it is the same behavior that we have originally with #2379 , and it is related to the Streamlit execution model, which executes the script on each rerun, which leads to redefining Enum defined there. 

So the workaround for this would be just defining your enum in another file, and import it to your app script. 

This should work correctly:

`colors.py`
```python
from enum import Enum, auto


class Color(Enum):
    RED = auto()
    BLACK = auto()
    YELLOW = auto()
```

`app.py`
```python
import streamlit as st
from colors import Color

if "color" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.color = Color.RED


st.code("st.session_state.color == Color.RED")
st.write(st.session_state.color == Color.RED)

st.code("st.session_state.color.value == Color.RED.value")
st.write(st.session_state.color.value == Color.RED.value)
```

Hey @rian-dolphin, this is actually expected behavior. I believe [this article](https://docs.streamlit.io/knowledge-base/using-streamlit/widget-updating-session-state) will explain the problem, but the changes recommended are:

1. Use a callback so that session state updates before the script/fragment is executed.
2. Don't supply the value in the text input. Streamlit identifies the text input by its arguments, since session state is changing, Streamlit regenerates the input. The solution is to supply a key and have the session state and the key be the same (or update it accordingly).

Closing this issue as this is expected behavior, but let me know if there's anything else you need.

Thanks for investigating @raethlein! I wonder if, rather than adding a new field to our script run context, we can just revert https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/commit/00cd56017e806f8947afb5bf29845a4d7166e167 instead (I think they may essentially boil down to being the same aside from the name of the field in script run context).

Thus, mutations to the `fragment_id_queue` have weird/unexpected consequences.

This is labeled as an enhancement but written as a bug report.

The issue described is expected behavior. The double-submit behavior happens when you declare a widget's default value (parameter) from Session State and then update that value in Session State from the output of the widget.

Instead, the recommended pattern is to assign a key to the widget directly and initialize that widget's value directly through its key. The example above would become:

```python
import streamlit as st

if 'initialized' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.part_number = ""
    st.session_state.forecast_frequency = ""
    st.session_state.number_of_forecast = 1
    st.session_state.initialized = True

col1, col2, col3, col4 = st.columns([1, 1, 1, 0.5])

with col1:
    st.text_input("Part Number", key="part_number")

with col2:
    frequency_options = ["", "Weekly", "Biweekly"]
    st.selectbox('Forecast Frequency', frequency_options, key="forecast_frequency")

with col3:
    forecast_number_options = [1,2,3,4]
    st.number_input(
        "Number of Forecast",
        min_value=1,
        max_value=len(forecast_number_options),
        key="number_of_forecast"
    )

with col4:
    st.write("")
    st.write("")
    button1 = st.button('Add Part')
```

So, I think this issue can be closed.

@nblackrjc Agreed that I'd like to be able to retrieve values from st.session_state within the callable if possible, but here's a workaround that I figured I'd share in case it's helpful to you:

Rather than directly providing the `get_data` callable to `st.download_button`, make it into a closure and provide its factory function to the button instead. Inside the factory function, copy any st.session_state values you need into regular local variables. Then, in `get_data()`, use those variables instead of the session state variables.

The outer function `get_data_factory()` is ran each time `st.download_button()` is created. However, since it returns a callable, the inner function `get_data()` isn't ran until the button is clicked. Thanks to Streamlit's execution model, assigning the `st.session_state` values to a local variable within the factory function should be functionally equivalent to being able to use the session_state values directly (unless you're changing the session state in a fragment that doesn't contain the download button, in which case the button won’t refresh and rebuild the closure).

```python
import streamlit as st

st.session_state['counter'] = 10

def get_data_factory() -> callable:
    def get_data():
        export_data = counter
        return str(export_data)
    counter=st.session_state['counter']
    return get_data

st.write(f"Counter value: {st.session_state['counter']}")
st.download_button(
    label="Download Counter",
    data=get_data_factory(),
    file_name="counter.txt",
)
```

approved_text: Second, for your use case — reading cookies on component initialization — `setStateValue` would be a better fit than `setTriggerValue`. All the [documented examples](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/custom-components/components-v2/examples) call `setTriggerValue` from event handlers, not on mount.

I do recognize now that two trigger-based widgets adjacent to each other would be like me writing `if st.button("1") and st.button("2"): ...`, both too ephemeral to happen at the same time.

For our use case, we do want the trigger-like behavior: the "cached" data could be stale. Per the above goals (clean/non-redundant session_state), I'm seeing the better design to be:
1. Have a session_state entry / wrapped variable accessor object; if the value is there, return cached value
2. If not there, run the component, stop until the value is returned (with merely a unique_key, not an ephemeral key?)
3. and then post-process and session_state cache the value as pleased
4. Optionally pre-load the values / queries on initial page load, to minimize logic interrupts
And whatever you do, don't depend on multiple simultaneous trigger-returned components.

setStateValue (or setting python component key) both invoke storing in session state, which shortcuts 1-4 (assuming you run the component on page load, stop if empty, and then post-access it only by session_state).

Following up on my analysis above with an actual browser reproduction, because I got something wrong in the meantime and the diagnosis turns out to be sharper than I described.

**First, a correction.** In my comment above I said the obvious test harness cannot exercise this, which is true, but I then went on to state on PR #16287 that the bug "does not reproduce on current `develop`." That was wrong, and I've retracted it there. `AppTest` cannot drive a fragment-scoped rerun, so it structurally cannot observe this — that's a limitation of the harness, not evidence the behaviour is gone.

**The behaviour reproduces.** Chromium against `be719acf27`, with a counter incremented *before* the button:

```python
@st.dialog("Dialog counting body runs")
def dialog_counting_body_runs() -> None:
    st.session_state.dlg_body_runs += 1        # work BEFORE the button
    st.write(f"body runs: {st.session_state.dlg_body_runs}")
    if st.button("Done", key="dlg_count_done"):
        st.rerun()
```

```
AFTER OPEN:  'body runs: 1'
AFTER DONE:  'outside body runs: 2'
```

The body executes **twice**, confirming @MattRCole's report.

**`st.rerun()` is not the cause.** This is the part I think is worth recording. I removed the `st.rerun()` call entirely — leaving `if st.button("Done"): pass` — and re-ran:

```
AFTER OPEN:  'body runs: 1'
AFTER CLICK: 'body runs: 2'    # dialog still open, st.rerun() absent
```

Still twice. The second execution is caused purely by the widget interaction triggering a fragment-scoped rerun of the dialog body (a dialog *is* a fragment, via `_fragment(...)` in `elements/dialog_decorator.py`). `st.rerun()` only determines what happens *after* that second execution — it closes the dialog. It plays no part in the re-execution itself.

So the issue title is slightly misleading: this is not specific to `st.rerun` in a button conditional. Any widget interaction inside a dialog re-executes everything above that widget. `st.rerun()` just makes it conspicuous, because the user's mental model is "closing" rather than "re-running".

**Why the pre-button work cannot be skipped.** The button's return value is only observable by executing the body up to it. Deciding to skip the fragment rerun would require knowing in advance that the body is going to request an app-scoped rerun, which is not knowable before running it. That's the same conclusion as my earlier comment, now with the cause correctly isolated.

**Coverage gap.** I also claimed on the PR that `e2e_playwright/st_dialog_test.py:656` already covered this. It does not. That test uses `dialog_with_rerun` (`st_dialog.py:276`), where the button is the *first* statement in the body, with no preceding work and no counter — so it verifies the dialog **closes** across fragment and full-app reruns, not that the body doesn't re-execute. This behaviour is genuinely untested.

**Where that leaves the decision**, unchanged in shape but now better evidenced:

1. If the intended contract is "a fragment body re-executes on any widget interaction, dialogs included," this is documentation — and the guidance is the `st.session_state` sentinel + early exit that @MattRCole is already using, or `on_click` (callbacks run before the script body). Worth saying explicitly in the `st.dialog` docs, since the failure mode is silent and expensive.
2. If the intended contract is "a dialog body should execute once per user-visible interaction," that is a semantics change to fragment reruns, and the opt-in `frozen`-style parameter from the original request is probably the least invasive shape.

I have a Playwright probe (`probe_13009.py` + counter assertions) that pins the current 2× behaviour and would serve as the regression test for either direction. Happy to send it as a PR — as a test documenting intended behaviour under option 1, or as the failing test under option 2. Just let me know which contract you want.

To be clear about scope: I am not proposing a fix here, because both options are product decisions in shared control-flow code.

Confirming this from a production incident — and it's a bit worse than "missing ScriptRunContext produces a warning": inside that thread, `st.session_state` reads return stale values and `@st.cache_data`-wrapped calls silently return whatever was already cached, **with no error and no warning**. Both just look like they worked.

Our incident: a `data=callable` on `st.download_button` called into functions that (transitively) read `@st.cache_data`-cached helpers. Because those calls run outside `ScriptRunContext`, they picked up cached results from a *different* request context — users occasionally downloaded a file that didn't match what they'd just generated on screen, with nothing in the logs to explain why. We only found the mechanism by tracing the full call graph of the callable, not just inspecting it — a lambda that looks pure can still be unsafe if anything it calls touches cached/session state indirectly.

We ended up moving off lazy `data=` entirely (eager bytes, pre-warmed at save time) because we couldn't make the callable's dependency tree provably free of session/cache reads. For anyone hitting this: if your callable calls anything that isn't a pure function of its arguments, the missing context isn't just a perf/warning issue, it's a correctness one.

The reset option in the expected behavior works at application level by including a data revision in the key. For the posted repro, change the dataframe key to:

```python
key=f"queue:{st.session_state['gen']}"
```

The existing refresh button already increments `gen`. On a refresh, this creates fresh selection state; an unrelated rerun keeps the same key. In an application, update the revision together with the served snapshot, including same-length reorders and value changes. Using only the row count misses those cases.

The same approach applies to the fixed-row editor:

```python
edited = st.data_editor(
    df,
    key=f"notes:{revision}",
    num_rows="fixed",
    disabled=["ticket", "status"],  # whichever columns are read-only in the app
    hide_index=True,
)
```

Here `revision` is the application's data version, and `df` is that version's snapshot. Interpret selection positions against that same snapshot. A new key clears unsaved edits as well as selection, so the UI needs to say that refreshes discard drafts; this implements reset, not selection preservation by record ID.

On Streamlit 1.64.0 / pandas 3.0.5 / Python 3.12.14, software-operated Chrome checks on macOS reproduced the wrong-ticket close in the original example and wrong-row note saving after a four-row reversal with a constant editor key. With revision keys, the checked sequences cleared the stale selection/draft, then successfully reselected and closed TICK-102 and re-edited and saved its note. Unchanged reruns retained selection/drafts, and subsequent insert/reorder operations retained saved notes. These were local browser checks, not a confirmation of the separate server-side validation concern.

The selected ticket can also be carried across a refresh at application level using the current public `selection_default` API. For your original example, replace the `event = st.dataframe(...)` line with this block, keeping it **before** the refresh and close buttons:

```python
ids = df['ticket'].tolist()
previous = st.session_state.get('selected_ticket')
default_rows = [ids.index(previous)] if previous in ids else []
event = st.dataframe(
    df,
    key=f"queue:{st.session_state['gen']}",
    on_select='rerun',
    selection_mode='single-row',
    lazy=False,
    selection_default={'selection': {'rows': default_rows}},
)
st.session_state['selected_ticket'] = (
    ids[event.selection.rows[0]] if event.selection.rows else None
)
```

The old position is resolved against the snapshot that produced it. The next revision gets a new widget key, with the same ticket ID mapped to its new position. A user changing or clearing selection replaces the stored ID; a missing ID clears it. IDs need to be unique and stable. Changing only `selection_default` with a constant key would not update existing selection.

The exact replacement passes the original select → insert → close sequence on Streamlit 1.64.0. A separate complete example using the same mapping also passed software-operated Chrome checks on macOS for insertion, repeated reordering, continued closing of TICK-102 and then TICK-103, source-value updates, hiding/removing the selected record, and explicit deselection. The visible checkbox/highlight followed the selected ticket.

This still needs application bookkeeping, and it does not supply a framework row-ID API or preserve pending `st.data_editor` edits. New keys can also reset display state such as scrolling/sorting. Your explicit apply-update idea remains useful for avoiding rows moving while someone is about to click.
